cards.s: Part B · LLM systems: the RAG service
cards.html:
rag-api answers employee questions from a (fictional) company handbook: vacation, sick leave, expenses, on-call. It embeds the question, retrieves the three most similar text chunks from Postgres with pgvector, and asks an LLM to answer only from those chunks. The design choice that makes CI possible is that every component sits behind a small interface with a free, deterministic fake for unit tests (Figure 17).

src/rag_api/embeddings.py (excerpt):

cards.s: Part B · LLM systems: the RAG service
cards.html:
class Embedder(Protocol):
    dim: int

    def embed(self, texts: list[str]) -> Vectors: ...

class HashEmbedder:
    """Bag-of-words hashed into a fixed-size vector (a test double)."""

    def __init__(self, dim: int = 256) -> None:
        self.dim = dim

    def embed(self, texts: list[str]) -> Vectors:
        out = np.zeros((len(texts), self.dim), dtype=np.float32)
        for row, text in enumerate(texts):
            for word in re.findall(r"[a-zäöüß0-9]+", text.lower()):
                h = int(hashlib.md5(word.encode()).hexdigest(), 16)
                out[row, h % self.dim] += 1.0
        norms = np.linalg.norm(out, axis=1, keepdims=True)
        return (out / np.maximum(norms, 1e-9)).astype(np.float32)

cards.s: Part B · LLM systems: the RAG service
cards.html: Embedder is a Protocol: any class with a dim and an embed() method fits. In unit tests, HashEmbedder turns words into hashed counts: meaningless as semantics, but deterministic, instant and free. In the evaluation, FastEmbedder runs the real model BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 locally on the CPU (ONNX, about 70 MB, no API key). The same pattern gives MemoryStore vs. PgVectorStore and FakeGenerator vs. ClaudeGenerator. Result: 15 unit tests run in under a second without network access, and one integration test runs against a real Postgres with pgvector.

cards.s: Part B · LLM systems: the RAG service
cards.html:
A golden set is a small, hand-curated list of questions with the expected source and a reference answer. It is the test data of an LLM system. Twenty good questions beat two hundred generated ones; include easy cases, paraphrases, questions that need the right paragraph, and some that mention German terms.

eval/golden.jsonl (two of 20 lines, wrapped for print):

{"id": "q04", "question": "When do I need a doctor's certificate when
  I am sick?", "expected_doc": "sick-leave", "reference": "From the
  fourth calendar day of illness."}
{"id": "q17", "question": "What documents do I need for the
  Anmeldung?", "expected_doc": "onboarding", "reference": "Passport
  and the Wohnungsgeberbestätigung."}

What if… the team tunes the system until the golden set is perfect?

cards.s: Part B · LLM systems: the RAG service
cards.html:
What happens: After a month of prompt tweaks, hit rate is 1.00 and faithfulness 1.00, but users report the same problems as before.

Why: The golden set became training data: every change was judged by it, so the system was fitted to these 20 questions. Same problem as tuning a model on its test set.

What you do: Keep a second, held-out set that only the nightly job uses and nobody looks at while tuning. Grow the golden set from production: every bad answer a user reports becomes a new golden question (after removing personal data), so the set follows real usage. And version the golden set in Git: a metric change caused by a golden-set change must be visible in the same PR.

cards.s: Part B · LLM systems: the RAG service
cards.html:
MetricMeaningThreshold
Hit rate@3Share of questions where the expected document is among the 3 retrieved chunks. Measures retrieval.≥ 0.90
MRRMean reciprocal rank: 1 if the right document is first, 1/2 if second, 1/3 if third, else 0, averaged.≥ 0.75
FaithfulnessShare of answers whose every claim is supported by the retrieved context, judged by an LLM. Measures hallucination.≥ 0.85

eval/run_eval.py (core loop):

cards.s: Part B · LLM systems: the RAG service
cards.html:
hits, rr, faithful = 0, 0.0, 0
    for item in golden:
        results = rag.retrieve(item["question"], args.k)
        docs = [chunk.doc for chunk, _ in results]
        hits += item["expected_doc"] in docs
        rr += reciprocal_rank(docs, item["expected_doc"])
        status = "HIT " if item["expected_doc"] in docs else "MISS"
        print(f"{status} {item['id']} {item['question'][:50]:<50} {docs}")
        if judge:
            answer = rag.answer(item["question"], args.k)
            context = [chunk.text for chunk, _ in results]
            faithful += judge.judge(context, answer.text).faithful

    n = len(golden)
    scores = {f"hit_rate_at_{args.k}": hits / n, "mrr": rr / n}
    if judge:
        scores["faithfulness"] = faithful / n
        print(f"judge cost this run: ${judge.spent_usd:.4f}")
    (HERE / "scores.json").write_text(json.dumps(scores, indent=2))

    limits = json.loads((HERE / "thresholds.json").read_text())
    failed = False
    for name, value in scores.items():
        ok = value >= limits[name]
        failed |= not ok
        print(
            f"{name:<14} {value:.3f}  (min {limits[name]})  "
            f"{'ok' if ok else 'FAIL'}"
        )
    return 1 if failed else 0

cards.s: Part B · LLM systems: the RAG service
cards.html:
Retrieval metrics need no LLM at all, so they are free and fast. The real run with the local embedding model:

terminal:

uv run python eval/run_eval.py

expected output:

HIT  q01 How many vacation days do full-time employees  ['vacation', …]
HIT  q07 Which days do I have to be in the Berlin office?  ['onboarding',
     'remote-work', 'expenses']
…
hit_rate_at_3  1.000  (min 0.9)  ok
mrr            0.975  (min 0.75)  ok

Look at q07: the right document is only in second place. That is exactly the kind of case a changed chunking strategy can push out of the top 3; the gate would catch it.

cards.s: Part B · LLM systems: the RAG service
cards.html:
Faithfulness uses an LLM as a judge. The judge sees the retrieved context and the answer, and returns a structured verdict. The SDK's messages.parse() validates the response against a Pydantic model, so the code never parses free text:

src/rag_api/judge.py (excerpt):

cards.s: Part B · LLM systems: the RAG service
cards.html:
def judge(self, context: list[str], answer: str) -> Verdict:
        prompt = JUDGE_PROMPT.format(
            context="\n\n".join(context), answer=answer
        )
        key = hashlib.sha256((self.model + prompt).encode()).hexdigest()
        cached = self.cache_dir / f"{key}.json"
        if cached.exists():  # same input as last time: free
            return Verdict.model_validate_json(cached.read_text())
        if self.spent_usd >= self.max_usd:
            raise RuntimeError(f"eval budget of ${self.max_usd} used up")

        response = self.client.messages.parse(
            model=self.model,
            max_tokens=300,
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
            output_format=Verdict,
        )
        price_in, price_out = PRICES.get(self.model, (5.0, 25.0))
        usage = response.usage
        self.spent_usd += (
            usage.input_tokens * price_in + usage.output_tokens * price_out
        ) / 1e6
        verdict = response.parsed_output
        if verdict is None:  # e.g. a refusal: count it as a failure
            verdict = Verdict(faithful=False, reason="no verdict")
        cached.write_text(json.dumps(verdict.model_dump()))
        return verdict

cards.s: Part B · LLM systems: the RAG service
cards.html:
Watch out: LLM judges have limits

A judge is a model too: it can be wrong, and it may favour answers that sound like its own. Spot-check its verdicts by hand, keep the judge prompt under version control (a prompt change changes the metric), and prefer a different or stronger model as judge when the stakes are high. Our companion code makes the cheap choice: by default the generator and the judge are the same small model (claude-haiku-5-5), which keeps CI cheap but means the judge grades its own family's answers. Set JUDGE_MODEL to a larger model for the nightly run (and add its price to PRICES in judge.py, or the budget check cannot count it); say this trade-off out loud in an interview. The judge path was tested with a mocked client; running it needs an ANTHROPIC_API_KEY.

cards.s: Part B · LLM systems: the RAG service
cards.html:
With 20 golden questions, each question is worth 5 percentage points. That turns the thresholds into simple counting rules:

Metric · thresholdQuestionsMeans in practice
hit rate ≥ 0.9020at most 2 retrieval misses
faithfulness ≥ 0.8520at most 3 unfaithful answers
faithfulness ≥ 0.855 (PR subset)no mistake allowed: 4 of 5 = 0.80 fails

What if… the faithfulness gate is red on a PR, green on the re-run?

What happens: On the 5-question PR subset, one answer was judged unfaithful. Re-run: green.

cards.s: Part B · LLM systems: the RAG service
cards.html:
Why: Two sources of noise meet: the generator and the judge are both LLMs, and their output can vary between calls for the same input. On 5 questions, a single changed verdict moves the metric by 0.20, across the threshold.

What you do: Do not make a 5-question LLM metric a hard gate. Options: use the subset as a warning (post the score as a PR comment) and gate hard only on the full set on main; or set a lower threshold for the subset; or run each question several times and use the majority verdict. Treat the retrieval metrics, which are deterministic, as the hard gate on PRs. And look at the failing question, not only the number: the judge's reason field says what it objected to.

cards.s: Part B · LLM systems: the RAG service
cards.html:
What if… we switch to a better embedding model?

What happens: You change BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 (384 dimensions) to a model with 768 dimensions. Unit tests pass (they use the fake embedder). The service starts and every query fails with pgvector's expected 384 dimensions, not 768. With a model of the same size the failure is worse: no error, just bad results, because question vectors and stored chunk vectors now come from different models and are not comparable.

Why: Vectors from different embedding models live in different spaces. Changing the model means re-embedding the whole corpus.

cards.s: Part B · LLM systems: the RAG service
cards.html: What you do: Treat the embedding model as part of the index version: store the model name with the index (a table per model, or a column), have the service refuse to start when they differ, and build the new index before switching (blue-green for data: build chunks_v2, evaluate it with the golden set in CI, then switch reads). The integration test against real pgvector catches the dimension case; the evaluation gate catches the silent case.

cards.s: Controlling LLM costs in CI
cards.html:
Every faithfulness run calls the LLM twice per question (answer + verdict). With Claude Haiku 5.5 at 0.10 USD per million input tokens and 0.50 USD per million output tokens (November 2026 list prices; check before relying on them), a full run of 20 questions with about 700 input tokens per call costs well under one cent. That is cheap, but a team with 50 PRs a day, a bigger golden set and a larger model pays real money, and an accidental loop can burn a budget. The pipeline therefore uses five levers (Figure 18):

  1. Free checks first. Retrieval metrics run on every PR; the paid job

needs: the free one.

cards.s: Controlling LLM costs in CI
cards.html:
1. Run expensive checks deliberately. Faithfulness runs on main, nightly, and on PRs only when a maintainer adds the label

llm-eval, and then only on 5 questions.

  1. Cache. Answers and verdicts are cached on disk, keyed by a hash of model + prompt, and the cache is restored with actions/cache. An unchanged question with unchanged context costs nothing.
  2. Judge budget cap. --max-usd 0.50 makes the judge raise an error once its estimated spend reaches the cap. Two honest limits: it counts only the judge's calls, not the generator's, and it checks before each call, so the last call can overshoot slightly. A production version tracks both clients in one budget object.
  3. Small, cheap models for judge and generator in CI, and token limits (max_tokens) on every call.

cards.s: Controlling LLM costs in CI
cards.html: .github/workflows/rag-eval.yml (faithfulness job):

cards.s: Controlling LLM costs in CI
cards.html:
faithfulness:                 # costs money: run it deliberately
    needs: retrieval
    if: >-
      github.event_name != 'pull_request' ||
      contains(github.event.pull_request.labels.*.name, 'llm-eval')
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    services:
      postgres:
        image: pgvector/pgvector:pg17
        env:
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: postgres
        ports: ["5432:5432"]
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "pg_isready -U postgres"
          --health-interval 5s --health-retries 10
    env:
      LLM: claude
      LLM_CACHE_DIR: eval/.cache/llm
      ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
      # 5 questions on labelled PRs, the full set on main and nightly
      LIMIT: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' && '5' || '20' }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v10.3.3
        with:
          enable-cache: true
      - run: uv sync --locked
      - uses: actions/cache@v6
        with:
          path: .cache/fastembed
          key: fastembed-bge-small-en-v1.5
      - name: Reuse earlier LLM answers and verdicts
        uses: actions/cache@v6
        with:
          path: eval/.cache
          key: llm-${{ hashFiles('eval/**', 'docs/**', 'src/**') }}
          restore-keys: llm-
      - name: Faithfulness gate (LLM-as-judge, max 0.50 USD)
        run: >
          uv run python eval/run_eval.py --faithfulness
          --limit "$LIMIT" --max-usd 0.50
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        if: always()
        with:
          name: rag-scores
          path: eval/scores.json

cards.s: Controlling LLM costs in CI
cards.html:
What if… I raise max_tokens and the eval results do not change?

What happens: Some answers were cut off, so you raise max_tokens in rag_api/llm.py from 400 to 800 and run the evaluation in CI. You get exactly the same, still truncated answers, at zero cost.

cards.s: Controlling LLM costs in CI
cards.html:
Why: Read the cache key in rag_api/llm.py: sha256(model + prompt). The prompt includes the question and the retrieved context, so changed documents or a changed prompt template invalidate the cache automatically. But max_tokens (and any other request parameter, such as a system prompt passed separately) is not part of the key, so the old answers are served from the cache. This gap is in our own code, and it is typical: a cache key must contain everything that influences the result.

What you do: Build the key from every request parameter, for example json.dumps({"model": …, "prompt": …, "max_tokens": …}, sort_keys=True). When in doubt, delete the CI cache (Actions → Caches).

What if… the LLM provider has an outage during CI?

cards.s: Controlling LLM costs in CI
cards.html:
What happens: The faithfulness job fails with 529 overloaded or a timeout. Nobody on main can merge, although nothing in the code is wrong.

What you do: Separate "the model is bad" from "the API was unavailable". The SDK already retries transient errors (max_retries); on top of that, catch API errors in the eval script and exit with a distinct status, and let the workflow mark that run as skipped with a warning instead of failed. Do not make a paid, external check a required PR check; the free retrieval gate is. The nightly run will catch up.

cards.s: Controlling LLM costs in CI
cards.html: The services: block (lines 59–67) starts a real Postgres with the pgvector extension next to the job, the standard way to give CI a database. The if: (lines 54–56) implements lever 2, the expression on line 73 picks the subset size, and lines 84–89 restore the cache.

cards.s: Operating ML pipelines over time
cards.html: Scheduled workflows. on: schedule: - cron: "30 2 * * *" runs a workflow every night at 02:30 UTC (cron fields: minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week). Use schedules for things that can break without a commit: nightly full evaluation, data validation against the latest upstream data, weekly retraining. Schedules run on the default branch only, may start a few minutes late, and GitHub disables them in public repositories after 60 days without activity.

cards.s: Operating ML pipelines over time
cards.html: Data versioning with DVC. Our CSV is small enough for Git. Real training data is not. DVC (Data Version Control) stores large files in S3 or similar and commits only a small pointer file (data.csv.dvc with a hash) to Git. dvc pull in CI fetches exactly the data version of that commit, so code, data and model stay linked. Alternatives: dated, immutable snapshots in S3, or table formats with time travel (Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg).

cards.s: Operating ML pipelines over time
cards.html: Model cards and changelogs. A model card is a short document shipped with each model: intended use, training data, metrics per segment, known limitations, fairness considerations. (We dropped the personal_status column of the German Credit data because it encodes sex; a model card is where you say so.) Generate the metrics part in CI from metrics.json and attach it to the release, next to a changelog generated from Conventional Commits.
